questions.q: Farida studies how water flows underground and wonders whether a similar question can be asked about how water climbs a tall tree. Gopal says, 'If the underground-water idea cannot answer the tree question, it is of no use to the study of plants.' Heena says, 'It may inspire a discovery about trees, or at least let us ask the question.' Which view matches how the chapter describes ideas from one area of science meeting another?
questions.a: Heena's: an idea in one area may inspire a discovery in another, or at least allow a question there
o: Heena's: an idea in one area may inspire a discovery in another, or at least allow a question there
Gopal's: an idea from one area is of use in another only if it can fully answer the question there
Neither: the chapter keeps physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences apart, so no idea passes between them
Neither: the chapter lets an idea pass between areas only when both questions sit in the same chapter

questions.q: Kavya says, 'If the chapter wants us to step out of the book, then the book itself is not needed.' (a) Using what the chapter says about its own chapters and activities, show that the book still has a job. (b) Suggest one thing Kavya should read in the book and one thing she should do outside it to learn about the monsoon.
questions.a: (a) The chapter says each chapter builds on what you already know, and the book also has topics that need careful thinking alongside the observations and experiments it asks for, so it is not discarded. (b) For example: read how water evaporates and falls as rain (book); measure the rain in an open can after each shower for a week (outside).
s: Part (a): each chapter builds on earlier knowledge / the book has topics needing careful thinking beside the experiments
Part (b): one sensible reading task and one outdoor activity on the monsoon

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the chapter idea it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. Three students fold planes with a sharp, a medium and a blunt nose and throw each from one spot to compare how far each flies  2. A group's first test matches their guess, yet they plan a second test with a different paper weight  3. A school measures how much waste each of its events creates and tests a reusable-cup scheme  4. A student asked why some fruits are sour now asks how a plant makes the fruit
Column II: a. Science can help address environmental challenges  b. Scientific ideas in one area allow us to ask questions in another  c. Experiments that confirm what we expect may lead to more experiments and questions  d. Activities and experiments are stepping stones to a deeper understanding

The Eco Club of a school in Thrissur notices that the rainwater pit in the school yard overflows after some rains. Rohan proposes reading three websites on drainage and summarising them. Swati proposes keeping an open can in the yard, noting each day's rainfall and marking the days the pit overflowed. After three weeks Swati's record matches the club's guess: the pit overflows after heavy rain. Tara says, 'The guess is confirmed, so we close the project.' The caretaker adds that on some of those days the club itself had swept dry leaves into the pit's mouth.
(a) Whose plan follows the chapter's call to step out of the book, and what does the chapter say such experiences are to a deeper understanding?
(b) What does the chapter say about experiments that seem to confirm what we expect, and what should the club do about Tara's suggestion?
(c) Which of the two links the chapter draws between human activities and the world does the caretaker's remark show, and how?
(d) The club can fund one more activity: (i) repeat the rain record for another three weeks, or (ii) record the leaf-sweeping days along with the rain. Choose one and say what the other could not have told the club.
questions.a: (a) Swati's plan; activities and experiments are stepping stones to a deeper understanding of the environment. (b) Even experiments that seem to confirm what we expect may lead to additional questions needing more experiments, so the club should not close the project but ask what else matters. (c) Human activities are linked to what happens in the natural world: sweeping leaves into the pit's mouth may block it and change what happens in rain. (d) Either with reasons: (ii) separates rain from leaf-blocking as causes; (i) checks that the pattern repeats but cannot say whether the club's own sweeping matters; the other choice cannot answer what the first one does.
s: Part (a): Swati's plan, with activities and experiments as stepping stones to deeper understanding
Part (b): confirming results can raise further questions needing more experiments, so do not close
Part (c): the link between human activities and the natural world, shown by the leaf-sweeping
Part (d): chooses one activity and states what the other could not have told the club

questions.q: Sonal says, 'The chapter calls activities and experiments stepping stones, so reading the results of the book's activities gives me the same understanding as doing them.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter asks us to step out of the book (and perhaps the classroom) and experience the world through activities and experiments; the stepping stones are those experiences. It also says even experiments that seem to confirm what we expect can lead to additional questions, and such questions come to the person who does the experiment, not to one who only reads a result.
s: Verdict: No, the claim does not follow
Evidence: the chapter asks us to step out of the book and experience the world through activities and experiments
Reason: the stepping stones are the experiences themselves, and new questions arise from doing, which reading results does not give

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter asks students to step out of the book and the classroom to experience the world through activities and experiments.
Reason (R): The chapter holds that the book and the classroom alone are enough for a deeper understanding of the environment.
questions.a: Assertion is true but Reason is false
o: Assertion is true but Reason is false
Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is false but Reason is true

questions.q: A student writes three questions about a paper plane: (i) 'How many sheets make a pack of 100 planes?' (ii) 'How does the plane stay in the air for a few seconds?' (iii) 'What pattern is there in how the distance flown changes as the nose is made sharper in steps?' (a) Which two are of the kinds the chapter says Grade 7 asks? (b) Name the kind each of those two belongs to, using the chapter's three kinds of deeper questions.
questions.a: (a) Questions (ii) and (iii). (b) (ii) is a 'How do things work?' question; (iii) is a 'What can we learn from the patterns we see?' question. Question (i) is only a counting question.
s: Part (a): picks (ii) and (iii) and leaves out the counting question
Part (b): (ii) as 'how do things work' and (iii) as 'what can we learn from patterns'

questions.q: After a first test shows that a sharp-nosed plane flies farther, Imran follows the chapter's remark that a confirming result can lead to more experiments. He now tries 3 nose shapes (blunt, medium, sharp) with 2 paper weights (thin, thick) and throws each combination 5 times. The total number of throws is ___.

Meera says, 'Counting the days the drain overflowed is a good start, but the questions the chapter wants Grade 7 students to ask go further, to why the pattern appears and what it teaches us.' Is Meera right? Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says that in Grade 7 we try to ask deeper questions: how do things work, why do events happen the way they do, and what can we learn from the patterns we see in nature. A count of overflow days gives a pattern; asking why it appears and what it teaches us is the step the chapter points to.
s: Verdict: Meera is right
Evidence: the chapter's deeper questions (how things work, why events happen, what patterns teach)
Applies it: the count of days is the pattern; the why and the lesson are the further questions

questions.q: A Class 7 teacher in Surat asks, 'Why do the potted plants on the terrace dry out sooner than those in the veranda?' Four students suggest what to do. Which suggestion best follows the chapter's call to experience the world through an activity that is a stepping stone to a deeper understanding of this question?
questions.a: Keep two identical pots, equally watered, one on the terrace and one in the veranda, and note each one's dampness at noon daily
o: Keep two identical pots, equally watered, one on the terrace and one in the veranda, and note each one's dampness at noon daily
Count how many pots stand on the terrace and how many in the veranda, and draw a bar chart of the two counts for the notice board
Paint the terrace pots in bright colours and hold a class vote on which row of pots looks the best
Read two gardening books on watering plants and write a summary of what the books say about each plant

questions.q: True or False: Lata's first test of her guess that a sharp-nosed plane flies farther gives exactly the result she expected. The chapter would still treat it as sensible for her to plan more experiments. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that even experiments that seem to confirm what we think will happen might lead to additional questions that need more experiments.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: confirming experiments can lead to additional questions and more experiments

questions.q:
A school in Hubballi notices stray dogs gathering near its gate. Three students propose plans. Meena: read three newspaper reports on stray dogs and write a summary. Nikhil: count the dogs at the gate every morning for three weeks and note whether the bin there is full that morning. Om: ask the watchman for the answer and use it. Nikhil's counts show more dogs on mornings when the bin is full, as he had expected.
(a) Which plan follows the chapter's advice to step out of the book and the classroom, and what does that advice offer?
(b) What does the chapter say about a result that matches what we expected, and what should Nikhil do next?
(c) The chapter says human activities are linked to what happens in the natural world. Show one such link in this problem.
(d) Besides discovery, the chapter says science is about something else. Name it and say what Nikhil could do with his finding to act on it.
(e) Write one question about a pattern that Nikhil's records could be used to ask.
questions.a: (a) Nikhil's plan; activities and experiments are stepping stones to a deeper understanding of our surroundings. (b) Even results that confirm what we expect may lead to additional questions needing more experiments, so Nikhil should test further, for example whether emptying the bin earlier lowers the count. (c) A human activity (leaving waste in the bin) is linked to what happens among animals around the school. (d) Responsibility; he could share his counts and suggest emptying the bin before school starts. (e) For example: 'What pattern is there between how full the bin is and how many dogs come, and why?'
s: Part (a): Nikhil's plan, and activities as stepping stones to deeper understanding
Part (b): confirming results can lead to more questions; names a further test
Part (c): a link between a human activity and the natural world around the school
Part (d): responsibility, with an action based on his finding
Part (e): a question of the 'patterns' kind drawn from his records

questions.q: Students of a Bhopal school notice that the bins overflow with plastic wrappers after every school event. They test a plan with a reusable-cup counter and find less waste. Their teacher links their work to the chapter. Which conclusion goes beyond what the chapter says?
questions.a: Because one school cut its waste, science has now ensured a sustainable world
o: Because one school cut its waste, science has now ensured a sustainable world
Their event waste shows a link between a human activity and what happens in the natural surroundings
Their tested plan is the kind of role the chapter says science can play with environmental challenges
Their finding about their own school is connected to the society that the school belongs to

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter.
Statement 1: According to the chapter, the world of science covers everything, small and large, near and far.
Statement 2: Because physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences appear as different chapters, the chapter says their ideas stay separate.
Statement 3: The chapter says human activities are linked to what happens in the natural world and are connected to the society we live in.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Priya says, 'The Grade 7 book has nothing to do with the Grade 6 book.' (a) Give one place in this chapter where it looks back to Grade 6. (b) Write one deeper question about rain, of the kind the chapter says Grade 7 asks, that cannot be answered by simply naming something.
questions.a: (a) 'Science, as we said in Grade 6, is a process' (or: just as we had said in Grade 6, the fields are all interconnected). (b) For example: 'Why does the drain overflow only after heavy rain?' or 'What pattern is there in the days when it rains?'
s: Part (a): a sentence that refers back to Grade 6 (science is a process; fields are interconnected)
Part (b): a rain question of the how/why/pattern kind, not a naming question

questions.q: The chapter says scientific ideas in one area often inspire discoveries in another, or at least allow us to ask questions in another. (a) Pick two topics that the chapter mentions from two different fields of science (for example sour fruits, water flowing underground, a lamp glowing, or whether plants need food) and name the field of each. (b) Write one question about the second topic that the first topic makes possible. (c) Say whether you expect your question to 'inspire a discovery' or only 'allow a question', and why. (d) Describe a simple activity outside the book that would test your question. (e) Say what a result that matches your guess could still lead to, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Marked on the student's own reasoning. For example: (a) sour fruits (chemistry/materials) and whether plants need food (biology). (b) Is the sourness of a fruit related to what the plant takes in to grow? (c) Only allow a question, because the sourness idea does not by itself say how a plant makes the fruit. (d) Taste unripe and ripe fruit of one tree on several days and note any change. (e) Additional questions and more experiments.
s: Part (a): two topics from the chapter belonging to two different fields
Part (b): a question about the second topic that the first topic makes possible
Part (c): says discovery or only a question, with a reason
Part (d): a workable activity outside the book that tests the question
Part (e): a matching result can still lead to more questions and experiments

questions.q:
The Eco Club of a school in Mysuru counted the plastic cups left in the school field in four weeks. Week 1: Sports Day, 900 visitors, water served in steel jugs and steel glasses, 40 cups found. Week 2: no event, 35 cups. Week 3: Annual Day, 400 visitors, tea and juice served in plastic cups, 90 cups found. Week 4: no event, 45 cups. The club had guessed, 'The bigger the crowd, the more cups.' Proposal X: no plastic cups at any event; the school buys 500 steel tumblers at ₹60 each. Proposal Y: a cleaning team collects the cups after each event at ₹1,500 per event; the school holds 6 events a year.
(a) Work out the cups found per 100 visitors at the two events. Does the record support the club's guess?
(b) The chapter says results can lead to more questions. State the next question the club should ask and one record it should start keeping.
(c) Name the two things the chapter says human activities are linked to, and give one example of each from this record.
(d) Compare the one-time cost of X with the cost of Y over one year, then choose a proposal and state one cost or risk of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Sports Day: 40/900 x 100 = about 4.4 cups per 100 visitors; Annual Day: 90/400 x 100 = 22.5 per 100. The guess is not supported: the larger crowd left fewer cups per visitor. (b) For example: 'What was different about the way the two events served drinks?' and keep a record of what was served in each event. (c) The natural world (cups left in the field) and the society we live in (the school community that bears the cleaning and cost). (d) X: 500 x 60 = Rs 30,000 once; Y: 1,500 x 6 = Rs 9,000 a year. Either with reasons: X tackles the source, since steel-served Sports Day gave only about 4.4 per 100 visitors, but costs about 3.3 years of Y and needs washing; Y is cheaper per year but the cups reach the field first.
s: Part (a): 4.4 and 22.5 per 100 visitors, guess not supported
Part (b): a next question about how drinks were served and a record to keep
Part (c): natural world and society, one example of each from the record
Part (d): Rs 30,000 versus Rs 9,000 a year, a choice with a stated cost or risk

questions.q: Hema's friend says, 'I now see that human activities are linked to what happens in nature.' Describe a situation from your school or town that could lead a student to say this, and write one question she could ask next.
questions.a: Any sensible situation: for example, plastic cups left in the school field after a function that choke the drain. The link is that our activity changes something in the natural surroundings. A next question: 'How many cups are left after each event, and what can reduce it?'
s: Describes a believable situation of a human activity
Shows the link to the natural world
Writes a follow-up question

questions.q: A student says, 'A sustainable world is a job for the government; science only explains how things work.' (a) Which role does the chapter say science can play? (b) Write one activity a Class 7 student could do in her school that fits this role, and say what she would measure.
questions.a: (a) Science can play a role in addressing environmental challenges and help in creating a more sustainable world. (b) For example: weigh the canteen's waste every day for a week to see which day creates most.
s: Part (a): the role in addressing environmental challenges / a more sustainable world
Part (b): a school activity that fits, with what is measured

questions.q: The chapter begins its tour with two questions about everyday things: why are some fruits sour, and what happens when we wash a haldi stain on a school uniform. (a) Which of the two is a 'why' question and which is a 'what happens' question? (b) Reword the 'what happens' question into one of the 'what can we learn from patterns' kind, using stains of different foods.
questions.a: (a) The sour fruits question asks why; the haldi stain question asks what happens. (b) For example: 'What pattern is there in how easily stains of turmeric, tea and ink wash out, and what does it tell us about them?'
s: Part (a): sour fruits as the why question, haldi stain as the what-happens question
Part (b): a pattern question that compares stains of different foods

questions.q: In a rainy month a Kochi school's drain overflowed only on days of heavy rain, and Group B has recorded this for the whole month. Which follow-up question is of the kind the chapter says Grade 7 asks about patterns we see in nature?
questions.a: What does the repeated link between heavy rain and overflow teach us about how this drain copes with water?
o: What does the repeated link between heavy rain and overflow teach us about how this drain copes with water?
What is the name of the pipe that carries water from this school drain to the main drain on the road outside?
How many millimetres of rain fell on the wettest day of the month in the whole district, according to the weather office?
On how many days of the month did the sweeper clear the drain, according to the school's cleaning register?

questions.q: A student writes the chapter's tour as a chain of questions, giving the reason for each move from one topic to the next. Which chain follows what the chapter says?
questions.a: Lamp glow → metals and non-metals; a battery that runs out → kinds of changes; changes sped by heat → how heat flows; the Sun's heat on seas → water's journey
o: Lamp glow → metals and non-metals; a battery that runs out → kinds of changes; changes sped by heat → how heat flows; the Sun's heat on seas → water's journey
Lamp glow → how heat flows (lamps give off heat); a battery that runs out → metals and non-metals; changes sped by heat → water's journey; the Sun's heat on seas → kinds of changes
Lamp glow → kinds of changes; a battery that runs out → how heat flows (batteries get hot); changes sped by heat → metals and non-metals; the Sun's heat on seas → water's journey
Lamp glow → metals and non-metals; a battery that runs out → water's journey (batteries hold water); changes sped by heat → kinds of changes; the Sun's heat on seas → how heat flows

questions.q: The chapter begins with everyday property questions: why are some fruits sour, and what happens when we wash a haldi stain on a school uniform. (a) According to the chapter, what kind of things does it start with, and why are they good starting points for questions? (b) Write a similar property question about a kitchen material of your own that you could test at home.
questions.a: (a) Properties of materials around us, mostly things we experience but perhaps never ask questions about, so there is something to wonder about in the ordinary. (b) For example: 'Why does salt vanish in water but sand does not?'
s: Part (a): the things we experience but perhaps never ask questions about
Part (b): a testable property question about a kitchen material

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with the topic of the tour in Column II that it belongs to or leads to.
Column I: 1. A mango ripens on the tree and a rock slowly breaks into pebbles  2. The Sun's heat evaporates water from the seas  3. Some changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated  4. A lamp glows with some materials in the circuit and not with others
Column II: a. The question of how heat flows  b. The journey of water through rain and the ground  c. Classifying materials as metals and non-metals  d. The question of which changes can be reversed and which cannot

The canteen of a school in Kolhapur must keep ice for sherbet through a 100-minute sports-day programme. A trial with the same amount of ice in each of three containers, in the same warm room, gave these times before the ice melted completely: open steel glass, 15 minutes; closed steel box, 45 minutes; thermos flask, 150 minutes. A glass costs ₹30, a box ₹120 and a flask ₹400. Fresh ice can be put in exactly when the old ice has melted, but each refill costs ₹40 of a helper's time. The canteen has ₹400.
(a) Using the chapter's idea of heat flowing into the ice, say what fraction of the glass's heat per minute flowed into the ice in the closed box.
(b) A volunteer moves the open glass from the shade into the sun. Predict whether the 15 minutes becomes shorter or longer, and give the chapter's reason.
(c) Work out the total cost of each container if it must last the whole programme, counting refills.
(d) Choose a plan within ₹400 and state one cost or risk of your choice.
questions.a: (a) The same ice needs the same heat, so heat flow per minute is in the ratio of the times: 15/45 = 1/3 of the glass's. (b) Shorter: more heat flows into the ice from the Sun, and the chapter says changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated. (c) Glass: 15 min each, so 6 refills: 30 + 240 = Rs 270. Box: 2 refills (at 45 and 90 min): 120 + 80 = Rs 200. Flask: 150 min, no refill: Rs 400. (d) Either with reasons: the box at Rs 200 is cheapest and leaves money, but needs a helper at 45 and 90 min and a late refill warms the sherbet; the flask uses the whole Rs 400 but needs no helper.
s: Part (a): one third, from the ratio of melting times for the same ice
Part (b): shorter, because more heat flows in from the Sun and heating speeds the change
Part (c): Rs 270, Rs 200 and Rs 400
Part (d): a plan within Rs 400 with a stated cost or risk

questions.q: Dinesh says, 'The chapter proves its topics must come in this order: properties of materials, changes, heat, then water. No other order is possible.' Test his claim against the chapter, using one link it actually states between neighbouring topics.
questions.a: No. The chapter takes a tour and links neighbouring topics with statements: for example, since a torch battery runs out, it explores what kinds of changes happen; and since some changes happen or happen faster when heated, it looks at how heat flows. It nowhere says no other order is possible; a link between neighbours is not a proof of a fixed order.
s: Verdict: No, the claim goes beyond the chapter
Quotes one stated link (battery to changes, or heated changes to heat flow)
Says a link between neighbours does not make the order the only possible one

questions.q: Geeta's village is 400 km from the nearest sea, and her well fills after the monsoon. She says, 'This water must have been sea water that evaporated and fell here.' Which statement is the strongest one the chapter lets her make?
questions.a: The Sun's heat evaporates sea water, which falls as rain and perhaps trickles into the ground far away, so her well may hold it
o: The Sun's heat evaporates sea water, which falls as rain and perhaps trickles into the ground far away, so her well may hold it
Her claim is exactly what the chapter says: rain that trickles into the ground does so only at the place where the sea water rose
Her claim is wrong, since the chapter says water evaporates from the seas but never falls on land as rain at all
Her claim is certain, since the chapter says rain trickles into the ground only after flowing back to the sea through rivers

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's tour, the topic of how heat flows comes before the topic of changes in materials.
Reason (R): Some changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated.
questions.a: Assertion is false but Reason is true
o: Assertion is false but Reason is true
Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false

questions.q: Anil says, 'The journey of water has nothing to do with heat.' (a) Which words of the chapter show that he is wrong? (b) Which earlier topic of the tour do those same words connect the water topic to?
questions.a: (a) 'With the heat from the Sun, it evaporates from the seas' (and falls as rain). (b) The topic of how heat flows, together with the changes that happen or happen faster when things are heated.
s: Part (a): the Sun's heat makes water evaporate from the seas
Part (b): links the water topic back to heat (how heat flows / changes on heating)

questions.q: Ritu says, 'The lamp-glow test and the torch battery running out are the same topic of the chapter, because both are about materials.' Evaluate her claim in five marks: (a) what question the lamp-glow test asks and what the chapter says it leads to; (b) what the running-out battery leads the chapter to ask; (c) what the two share in the chapter; (d) whether the two are the same topic, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) What kind of materials we need to make a lamp glow; it leads to classifying materials by their properties, the world of metals and non-metals. (b) A torch battery runs out and cannot be used again, so the chapter explores what kinds of changes happen, some reversible and some not. (c) Both use a battery and both concern materials. (d) Not the same: the first asks about a property and classification; the second asks about a change over time and whether it can be reversed.
s: Part (a): lamp-glow question, leading to classification by properties and to metals and non-metals
Part (b): the battery that runs out, leading to kinds of changes and reversibility
Part (c): the battery and the materials they share
Part (d): verdict that they are different topics, with the reason (property and classification versus change and reversal)

questions.q: In a trial, an ice block melted in 15 minutes in an open steel glass and in 150 minutes in a thermos flask in the same room. As the same ice needs the same heat to melt, heat flowed into the ice in the flask ___ times more slowly than into the glass.

True or False: The chapter's lamp-glow question leads to classifying materials by their properties, and the world of metals and non-metals comes after it, so in the chapter's order sorting by a property comes before the names 'metal' and 'non-metal'. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the question of which materials make a lamp glow leads to classifying materials based on their properties, and that we then enter the world of metals and non-metals; the property comes first and the groups follow.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the lamp-glow question leads to classification by properties, and then to metals and non-metals

questions.q:
A village near Dehradun records its well's water as the depth of the water below the ground: April, 9 m; July, 8 m; September, 5 m; December, 6 m. The village is 400 km from the sea and its rain falls from June to September. The panchayat must decide whether to limit pump use from March to May. Farmer Ramesh says there is plenty of water because September's level is high; the Sarpanch points out that April's level was lowest.
(a) Between which two readings did the water rise fastest, at how many metres per month, and which step of the chapter's water journey is behind that rise?
(b) If the water kept falling after September at the September-to-December rate, how deep would it be by the following April (four months after December)? Assume the next April will be much like this April's 9 m, and say what the difference shows about a steady-rate guess.
(c) Using the chapter, say where the rain that raised the well may have started and what drove that first step.
(d) Decide whether pump use should be limited from March to May, and justify with the data and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) July to September: 3 m in 2 months = 1.5 m per month (April to July was only 1 m in 3 months, about 0.33 m per month). Rain trickling down into the ground. (b) Fall from September to December = 1 m in 3 months, about 0.33 m per month; December to April is 4 months, so 6 + 1.33 = about 7.3 m. If next April is like this April's 9 m, that is deeper, so the fall in the dry months is faster than a steady rate predicts. (c) It may have started as sea water evaporated by the heat of the Sun, falling as rain, perhaps far away from the sea. (d) Yes limiting is supported: the well is refilled only by the monsoon rain trickling down, April is the deepest reading and no refill comes in March to May; an argument against must weigh the farmers' summer needs against the data.
s: Part (a): July to September, 1.5 m per month, and rain trickling into the ground
Part (b): about 7.3 m against 9 m, so the dry-month fall is not steady
Part (c): sea water evaporated by the Sun's heat, falling as rain, perhaps far away
Part (d): a decision justified by the April reading and the monsoon refill

questions.q: Ajay says, 'A well 400 km from the nearest sea can have nothing to do with the sea.' Show, using the chapter's own sentences, that this cannot be held as certain, and name the word in the chapter that stops us from saying the well's water definitely came from the sea.
questions.a: The chapter says that with the heat from the Sun, water evaporates from the seas and falls as rain, perhaps trickling down into the ground somewhere far away. So sea water can end up underground far from the sea, and Ajay's 'nothing to do with' cannot be held. The word 'perhaps' means the chapter does not claim this particular well's water came from the sea.
s: Quotes the chain: evaporates from the seas, falls as rain, trickles into the ground
Shows that this can happen somewhere far away, so a distant well can be linked to the sea
Names 'perhaps' as the word that stops a definite claim

questions.q: After sports day, a class in Dehradun puts one ice cube on a steel plate in the sun and one on a steel plate in the shade and watches both melt. Which question about this activity belongs to the chapter's topic of how heat flows, rather than to its topics on changes, properties or water?
questions.a: How does the warmth of the sun-heated plate reach the ice and make it melt sooner?
o: How does the warmth of the sun-heated plate reach the ice and make it melt sooner?
Can the melted water be frozen again to give back the same ice cube, or is this a change that cannot be undone?
Is steel a material that makes a lamp glow when the plate is made part of a circuit with a battery?
Where does the water that spills from the plate go if it soaks into the ground far from the school?

questions.q: Hema writes: 'The Sun's heat evaporates water from the seas, and some changes happen faster when things are heated, so heat explains every change in the chapter's list: a battery running out, fruits ripening and rocks breaking into pebbles.' Is Hema right? Mark what is right and what goes too far.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter does say the Sun's heat evaporates water from the seas and that some changes happen, or happen faster, when heated. But it says only 'some', so 'every change' goes too far; it gives no heating cause for the run-out battery, which it uses to show a change that cannot be reversed.
s: Verdict: partly right
Credits the two statements the chapter makes (evaporation by the Sun's heat; some changes speed up on heating)
Corrects 'every' to 'some', using the battery that runs out

questions.q: The chapter says some changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated. In a test, a cut mango piece browns in 30 minutes in a sunny window and in 90 minutes in a shaded room. (a) How many times faster does it brown in the sun? (b) Does this one test show that every change in the chapter's list happens faster when heated? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 90/30 = 3 times faster. (b) No. One change was tested, and the chapter itself says only that some changes happen, or happen faster, when heated; it does not say all.
s: Part (a): 3 times
Part (b): no, one change tested, and the chapter says only 'some'

questions.q: A student draws the chapter's water journey as arrows: sea → evaporates → falls as rain → trickles into the ground → returns to the sea. (a) Which arrows does the chapter's sentence describe? (b) Which arrow does it not describe, and what question does that raise?
questions.a: (a) Sea to evaporation, evaporation to rain, and rain to trickling into the ground (perhaps far away). (b) The return to the sea is not described; it raises the question of where the water that trickles underground goes next.
s: Part (a): the first three arrows (evaporates, falls as rain, trickles into the ground)
Part (b): the return to the sea is not described, with a question it raises

questions.q: Naina's circuit test finds that a steel spoon, a copper wire and a coin make the lamp glow, while a plastic comb, a wooden ruler and a rubber band do not. According to the chapter, what does this kind of activity prepare her to do next?
questions.a: Sort materials into groups by this property, the step the chapter says leads into metals and non-metals
o: Sort materials into groups by this property, the step the chapter says leads into metals and non-metals
Decide for each material whether the change it goes through can be reversed, since reversibility is the next topic the chapter takes up
Work out how heat flows through each material when it is left in the sun, which is the next step the chapter takes in its tour
Trace how rain trickles through each material into the ground somewhere far away, the next topic the chapter takes up in its tour

questions.q: Arun says, 'Sourness of a fruit and the lamp-glow test are the same kind of property.' (a) Which phrase of the chapter shows that the battery-lamp-wire work looks for a different kind? (b) Name three objects you could test and what you would record for each to show that the result is a property of the material.
questions.a: (a) 'Other kinds of properties of materials'. (b) For example: steel spoon, plastic comb, coin; record 'lamp glows' or 'lamp does not glow' for each, using the same battery, lamp and wires so that only the material changes.
s: Part (a): 'other kinds of properties of materials'
Part (b): three objects with glow / no glow recorded, same circuit each time

questions.q: The chapter meets the melting of ice twice, once among the changes around us and once as an example of how heat flows. In five marks explain (a) what question each topic asks about the same ice, and (b) which of the two topics the chapter gives the melting of a glacier as an example of.
questions.a: (a) As a change: is this change one that can be reversed or not? As heat flow: how does heat flow into the ice, and why does it melt faster when warmer? (b) The glacier is named, together with the ice cube in a glass, as an example of how heat flows.
s: Names the changes topic and its question (can it be reversed or not)
Names the heat-flow topic and its question (how heat moves in)
Says the glacier is given as an example of how heat flows

questions.q:
Read the statements about the tour.
Statement 1: The chapter lists the melting of ice among the changes that cannot be reversed.
Statement 2: The chapter gives the melting of an ice cube in a glass and the melting of a glacier as examples of how heat flows.
Statement 3: The chapter says that with the heat from the Sun, water evaporates from the seas and falls as rain.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Meena's growth has slowed. Tests show she eats a full diet and breathes normally. Using the chapter's account of what animals need in order to grow, which of its named needs is still left to check?
questions.a: Whether blood is circulating the nutrients from her food all over her body
o: Whether blood is circulating the nutrients from her food all over her body
Whether she is eating enough food, since growth needs food
Whether she is breathing enough, since growth also needs breathing
Whether the plants near her home also breathe, since the chapter asks about plants

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says a clock or wrist watch tells us the time and how it passes, so it has already answered how we measure time and how fast something happens. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. After saying what a clock or watch does, the chapter asks, 'have you thought about how we measure time? And how fast does something happen?' It raises these as questions to think about, not as answered ones.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the chapter poses how we measure time and how fast something happens as questions after describing the clock

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the line of the chapter it illustrates in Column II.
Column I: 1. A doctor tells Chetan that growth needs food to be turned into nutrients and carried to every part of his body  2. A farmer in a field with a fixed stick guesses how many hours remain before sunset from where its shadow falls  3. A student explains the darkening of the Sun's disc at midday by a shadow cast by another body in the sky  4. A village gets street lights, so children can finish homework after dark
Column II: a. Early humans' way of telling the time  b. One of the many ways we have developed to generate light  c. Life processes essential to animals: eating, breathing and the circulation of nutrients  d. The Earth and the Moon can cast shadows, leading to eclipses

A Class 7 section in Nagpur recorded the heights of four students at the start of Class 6 and at the start of Class 7. A: 140 cm to 148 cm. B: 145 cm to 147 cm. C: 138 cm to 149 cm. D: 150 cm to 154 cm. Ms Rao notes that B grew least and wants to find out why.
(a) The chapter says our bodies change rapidly around the middle-school years. Work out the mean growth of the four students and name those who grew by more than the mean.
(b) Ms Rao first checks how much B eats. Which life process of the chapter is she testing, and which other process in the chapter links food to the whole body, so that eating alone cannot be the whole story?
(c) Give D's rank among the four by height at the start of Class 7 and by growth during the year, and say what the difference shows.
(d) Ms Rao can (i) record B's meals for two weeks or (ii) ask the school doctor to check B's breathing and blood circulation. Choose one to do first and give a reason from the chapter and a cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Growth: A 8, B 2, C 11, D 4; mean = 25/4 = 6.25 cm. A and C grew more than the mean. (b) Eating; the circulation of the nutrients from the food by the blood all over the body (breathing is a third need). (c) D is 1st by height (154 cm) and 3rd by growth (4 cm, after C and A): the tallest student did not grow most, so height now does not show how much a body changed. (d) Either with reasons: (i) is cheap and quick and tests eating, but covers only one of the processes; (ii) covers breathing and circulation, the other two the chapter names, but takes time and may worry B.
s: Part (a): mean 6.25 cm; A and C above it
Part (b): eating, and the blood circulating the nutrients all over the body
Part (c): D is 1st by height and 3rd by growth; height now does not show how much the body changed
Part (d): a chosen first step with a reason from the chapter and a cost

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter says that day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun.
Reason (R): The chapter says that early humans used the position of shadows in the Sun to tell the time.
questions.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

questions.q: To use the idea of early humans, a class puts a pebble at the tip of a pole's shadow once every hour, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., including both 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. The class needs ___ pebbles.
Rhea says, 'Day and night happen because the Moon goes around the Earth.' Does the chapter support her? Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun. It lists the Moon going around the Earth with the Earth's rotation and the Earth's movement round the Sun as things we need to know to understand all of this, but it does not name the Moon's movement as the cause of day and night.
s: Verdict: not supported by the chapter
Reason: day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun
Notes that the Moon's movement is listed with the other two movements among the things to understand, and is not named as the cause of day and night

questions.q: Ravi times two toy cars over the same 2 m track by counting aloud. Car A takes 8 counts and car B takes 5 counts. (a) Work out each car's speed in metres per count. (b) Which of the chapter's two questions about time is Ravi answering?
questions.a: (a) Car A: 2/8 = 0.25 m per count; car B: 2/5 = 0.4 m per count. (b) 'How fast does something happen?'
s: Part (a): 0.25 m per count and 0.4 m per count
Part (b): how fast does something happen

questions.q: The chapter asks two questions about time: 'How do we measure time?' and 'How fast does something happen?' Pooja plans to let sand run through a small hole in a bottle and count how many bottles fill in the school day. Qasim plans to let two snails crawl along a 1 m board and compare how long each takes. Going by the main purpose of each plan, which pairing is right?
questions.a: Pooja's plan is about how we measure time; Qasim's is about how fast something happens
o: Pooja's plan is about how we measure time; Qasim's is about how fast something happens
Pooja's plan addresses how fast something happens; Qasim's addresses how we measure time
Both plans address only the question of how we measure time
Both plans address only the question of how fast something happens

questions.q:
Read the statements about light and shadows.
Statement 1: The chapter says light is useful only to help us see and to make shadow puppets.
Statement 2: The chapter says that day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun.
Statement 3: The chapter says the Earth and the Moon can cast shadows, leading to eclipses.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Reverse: the result reads, 'The class decides to ask the same kind of questions about plants that it asks about animals.' Describe a situation, using the chapter, that leads a class to this result, and write the two plant questions it would ask.
questions.a: A class watches a puppy eat, breathe and grow, and then notices that a seedling in a pot is also growing. Because the chapter names eating and breathing as processes of animals and asks 'Don't plants also need food to grow? Do they also breathe?', the class asks: 'How does the seedling get its food?' and 'Does it also breathe, and how?'
s: Describes a believable situation that puts an animal and a plant side by side
Links it to the animal processes the chapter names (eating and breathing)
Writes the two plant questions: how plants get food, and whether and how they breathe

questions.q: During a power cut at night, Chetan lights a candle beside a stick and says, 'I will tell the time from where the stick's shadow falls, as early humans did.' Why will this not work as it did for early humans?
questions.a: The early method read the Sun's moving shadow, but a candle stays fixed, so its shadow does not move with the hours
o: The early method read the Sun's moving shadow, but a candle stays fixed, so its shadow does not move with the hours
The early method read shadows made by the Moon, which a candle cannot copy because a candle gives off no light that could throw a shadow at all
Shadows can be cast only by daylight, so a candle in a dark room can never cast a shadow of the stick at all
Early humans needed a row of several sticks, because the shadow of a single stick cannot show the time of day

questions.q: True or False: The chapter's account of growth means that food alone is enough for a child to grow. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that to grow we have to eat and breathe, and that blood has to circulate the nutrients from the food all over the body, so growth needs these processes together.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: growth needs eating, breathing and the circulation of nutrients by blood

questions.q: Sneha says, 'The chapter says we have developed many ways to generate light, and that this gave us a very deep understanding of the universe.' Mark what is right and what goes too far.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter does say we have developed a lot of ways to generate light, so we can read at night. But it credits the deep understanding of the universe to asking questions about the nature of light, which it calls more important, not to the ways of generating light.
s: Verdict: partly right
Credits the true part: the chapter mentions many ways to generate light
Corrects the cause: the deep understanding came from asking questions about the nature of light

questions.q: Plan an activity on the school ground to find out how the position of a pole's shadow changes during the day. State (a) what you set up, (b) when you record, (c) what you record, (d) what pattern you expect and (e) one new question the results could raise.
questions.a: (a) A pole fixed in sunlit ground. (b) At regular times through the day. (c) Where the tip of the shadow falls, marked with a pebble. (d) The tip moves to a different place as the day goes on, so the position tells the time. (e) For example, 'Does the shadow follow the same path every sunny day?'
s: Part (a): a pole in the Sun
Part (b): regular times
Part (c): the position of the shadow tip
Part (d): the position changes with time, so it tells the time
Part (e): a sensible further question

questions.q:
Class 7B in Pune printed 300 notices for a sky-watching evening at ₹2 each. The notice says: 'To follow eclipses and day and night, learn that the Earth rotates on its axis and that the Moon goes around the Earth.' The teacher says one movement is missing. A rubber stamp adding the missing line costs ₹150 but fits only the 220 notices that have a blank margin; the other 80 have no space. Reprinting a notice costs ₹2 again. The class has ₹400 for the repair. The Principal's note says, 'Day and night happen because the Moon casts its shadow on the Earth.'
(a) Which movement is missing from the notice?
(b) Using the chapter, correct the Principal's note and say what the shadows of the Earth and the Moon lead to.
(c) Work out the cost of stamping the 220 and reprinting the other 80, and compare it with reprinting all 300.
(d) Choose full reprint, the stamp-and-reprint plan, or the stamp alone, and state one cost or risk of your choice.
questions.a: (a) The Earth going around the Sun. (b) Day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun, not on the Moon's shadow; the shadows cast by the Earth and the Moon lead to eclipses. (c) Stamp Rs 150 + reprint 80 x 2 = Rs 160 gives Rs 310; reprinting all 300 costs 300 x 2 = Rs 600, which is Rs 290 more. (d) Either with reasons: full reprint at Rs 600 is over the Rs 400 limit; the stamp-and-reprint plan costs Rs 310 and completes all 300 but uses most of the Rs 400 and needs two separate jobs; the stamp alone costs Rs 150 but 80 notices stay incomplete.
s: Part (a): the Earth going around the Sun
Part (b): day and night depend on light from the Sun; shadows of the Earth and Moon lead to eclipses
Part (c): Rs 310 against Rs 600
Part (d): a plan chosen with a stated cost or risk, checked against the Rs 400 limit

questions.q: The chapter lists three things animals need to grow: eating, breathing and blood circulating the nutrients. It asks plant questions about two of them. (a) Which of the three has no plant question in the chapter? (b) Write a plant question of the same style for it.
questions.a: (a) The blood circulating the nutrients from the food all over the body. (b) For example: 'How does food reach all the parts of a plant?'
s: Part (a): the circulation of nutrients
Part (b): a plant question in the style 'how do they ...?'

questions.q: A student sees the long shadow of her school building at evening and says, 'This is a small eclipse.' (a) Which bodies does the chapter say can cast the shadows that lead to eclipses? (b) Why does the chapter's wording not support calling the building's shadow an eclipse?
questions.a: (a) The Earth and the Moon. (b) The chapter keeps the word eclipse for the shadows cast by the Earth and the Moon; the shadow of an ordinary object in the Sun is the kind early humans read to tell the time.
s: Part (a): the Earth and the Moon
Part (b): eclipses come from Earth and Moon shadows, while an object's shadow is the kind used to tell the time

questions.q: Arvind says, 'We have lamps for the night and clocks for the time, so there is no need to study light and shadows now.' Argue for and against, then give a verdict. Use the chapter.
questions.a: For: we can generate light to read at night and watches tell the time. Against: questions about the nature of light gave a deep understanding of the universe, and shadows of the Earth and Moon lead to eclipses. Verdict: study is still needed because the chapter says light and shadows reach beyond the things at home.
s: Gives a point for Arvind's view from the chapter
Gives a point against: deep understanding of the universe
Gives a second point against: Earth and Moon shadows and eclipses
Gives a verdict
Justifies the verdict with the chapter

questions.q: The chapter says a clock or wrist watch tells us the time and how it passes. (a) Give one school-day example where you need 'the time' and one where you need 'how time passes'. (b) Explain why knowing the time of day alone does not tell us how fast a snail moves.
questions.a: (a) For example: knowing that it is 8.00 a.m. when the bell rings (the time); knowing that a period has lasted 40 minutes (how time passes). (b) Speed needs the distance covered and the time that passed while covering it, not just the time of day.
s: Part (a): one example of each, kept apart
Part (b): speed needs distance and the time that passed

questions.q:
Read the statements about life processes.
Statement 1: The chapter says our bodies are changing rapidly, especially around the middle-school years.
Statement 2: The chapter names eating, breathing and the circulation of nutrients by blood as life processes essential to animals.
Statement 3: The chapter answers, in this introduction, how plants get their food and whether they breathe.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
